name: Colin Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, have a bachelor’s degree and maintain ferry-ticketing software at a tech company as an experienced mid-level developer. I use AI every day to draft booking tests, but compare them with the passenger manifest. Bea works on a ferry deck, our children are grown, and higher developer pay has helped us rent with twelve months of expenses saved and plenty of nearby software jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the ferry-ticket team that a small AI shortcut may spot a duplicate booking, but a passenger still needs the right boat and departure time. I use AI every day to draft test bookings and compare them with the manifest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a bachelor’s degree and maintain this ticketing system as an experienced mid-level developer on higher pay. Bea works on a ferry deck, our children are grown, and we rent with twelve months of expenses saved and many other software employers nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking duplicate tickets against each Friday’s passenger manifest. We would save 250 monthly while both wages hold and repair the old shed roof rather than replace the shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about our jobs and bills here. A ticket can be duplicated on a screen, but one passenger cannot stand in two places on a boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What duplicate caused trouble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A family received two boarding codes for one seat, and the gate rejected both. I compared the manifest with the purchase record before the sailing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use AI every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me awkward booking cases fast. I still run the case against the actual boarding rules and have another developer review a live change.

say: I want **boarding codes** checked against the passenger manifest.
I use **AI daily** for draft tests and verify the sailing.
think: I have **twelve months saved** from higher developer pay and Bea’s ferry work.
I see **rent covered** while both current wages keep arriving.
do: **Save 250 monthly** while both wages hold; repair shed roof rather than replace shed.
S0.quote: A ticket can be duplicated on a screen, but one passenger cannot stand in two places on a boat.
fieldNote: His **mid-level coding** handles boarding rules rather than claiming captain or deck skills.
A **year of savings** supports security without assuming help from grown children.

steps.text: Check duplicate ferry tickets against passenger manifests each Friday
Save 250 monthly while both household wages continue
Repair old shed roof rather than replace the shed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking booking, checking and coding could handle many ticket cases, but a crew member should still settle a passenger left at the gate. I would want a named person to approve live boarding changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My developer hours could shrink if one person oversees automated bookings. Twelve months saved and nearby firms give me room, but Bea’s deck wage alone will not cover all our rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the manager for approved paid time to pilot an AI duplicate-ticket checker on archived bookings, with a ferry supervisor signing off errors. If approved, I’d test one wrong boarding code weekly; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local transport-software vacancies only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours and curious about the checker. The boat does not wait while we debug a passenger at the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the supervisor review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supervisor would compare my flagged booking with the manifest and the actual boarding rule. I would not turn on an AI gate decision from a test alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use live passengers in the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The old bookings would have names removed, and the paid trial would need approval before touching a live gate.

say: I want **crew sign-off** before an AI boarding change reaches a live ferry gate.
I want **archived tickets** tested before any real passenger uses the checker.
think: I could lose **paid developer hours** to automated booking.
I cannot make **Bea’s deck wage** cover all our bills.
do: **Pilot AI duplicate checker** weekly only with approved paid time, anonymized bookings and ferry supervisor sign-off.
**Search paid transport software** if hours fall and local vacancies cover rent and bills.
S1.quote: The boat does not wait while we debug a passenger at the gate.
fieldNote: His **new AI pilot** requires paid approval and a supervisor’s sign-off beyond existing daily test drafts.
The **local search** begins only if paid hours fall and a real vacancy covers bills.

steps.text: Pilot AI ticket checks weekly on archived nameless bookings only with paid approval and ferry-supervisor sign-off
Search paid local transport-software vacancies if hours fall and wages cover rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write our ticket code and settle routine boarding questions cheaper than our team. Robots moving ropes and working ferry decks may arrive around 2031, after our screen tasks change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my developer wage could end quickly despite years on this system. Twelve months saved gives us search time, but Bea’s deck work may face the next wave and cannot replace my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d postpone our planned patio work and ask for written notice of any developer cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local shore-ticket roles only if there are vacancies, I meet current safety requirements and wages cover rent and bills; I would not buy a boat to create work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing a steady wage. A boarding pass is not a pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would shore-ticket work last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know; AGI may do much of that too. I would take only an actual paid opening, not call it a safe career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for ferry work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would search local ferries and tech employers first. Bea’s vessel and our rented home are here, so I am not planning a move.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach ticket code first.
I expect **deck robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **developer wage** could end quickly.
I know **twelve months saved** buys time, not permanent income.
do: **Postpone patio work** and request written cut notice now.
**Apply for shore-ticket work** after 2028 loss only if qualified paid local vacancies cover rent and bills.
S2.quote: A boarding pass is not a pay slip.
fieldNote: His **shore-ticket option** may also face AGI and requires current safety rules and a paid vacancy.
He protects **rent savings** rather than buying a boat on speculation.

steps.text: Postpone planned patio work when developer cuts threaten
Apply for qualified paid local shore-ticket vacancies if displaced after 2028 and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us time to refresh ferry safety knowledge while ticket code changes. Robots on physical decks may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn current shore safety procedures while drawing developer pay, but an old ticketing job does not automatically qualify me. I would pay for a bounded course only if it protects our savings and a paid opening could use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d enrol in a shore-passenger safety course only if it is available, costs no more than 160 and leaves ten months of expenses saved. I’d practise an evacuation briefing weekly with the instructor; we would save 230 monthly while both wages hold, and after 2031 developer job loss I’d apply for paid local shore roles only if certified vacancies cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the code job but glad to test a real passenger-safety skill. A course card does not hold a ferry at the dock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the briefing cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practise the route to the muster point and the order for helping passengers with mobility needs. The instructor would correct my wording before I said it to a real crowd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course costs more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would wait or ask a hiring ferry whether it funds the course for a paid vacancy. I would not cut into the ten-month reserve for a guess.

say: I want **current shore safety** before AGI reaches ticket code in 2031.
I expect **deck robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I could learn **passenger safety** while developer pay lasts.
I need **ten months untouched** after a course fee.
do: **Enrol in shore course** only if available, useful for paid openings, fee at most 160 and ten-month reserve remains.
**Save 230 monthly** while both wages hold; apply for certified paid shore vacancies after 2031 loss only with bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious but testing** a bounded safety route.
S3.quote: A course card does not hold a ferry at the dock.
fieldNote: His **self-funded course** has a fee cap and reserve floor, with no promised job.
A **shore vacancy** still needs certification and bill-covering pay after any coding loss.

steps.text: Enrol in available shore-safety course only for relevant paid openings, at most 160, preserving ten-month reserve
Save 230 monthly while both household wages continue
Apply for certified paid local shore vacancies if displaced after 2031 and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives ferry firms time to make safe boarding plans and families time to check their money. Robots working physical decks may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still want paid work at 68 and have not verified a retirement amount. Twelve months saved gives us options, but future ferry roles and Bea’s deck shifts are not guaranteed forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep maintaining ticket code and save 240 monthly while both wages continue. I’d request a written retirement-income estimate and enrol in an available shore-safety course only if its fee stays at most 160 and ten months of expenses remain saved. If my developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local shore roles only if certified vacancies cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about later work but secure for the next few years. A timetable is useful only if a real boat and crew turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train before a vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use an affordable course only while our ten-month reserve remains intact. I would not assume it makes a paid shore job appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children fund the later plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have their own households, and Bea and I will use our pay and verified figures.

say: I want **verified income figures** before AGI reaches ticket code in 2036.
I expect **deck robots around 2039** to follow later.
think: I cannot assume **retirement income** without a written estimate.
I see **current bills secure** with twelve months saved.
do: **Maintain ticket code** and save 240 monthly while both wages hold; request written retirement-income estimate.
**Enrol in shore course** only if available, fee at most 160 and ten-month reserve intact.
**Seek paid shore vacancies** after 2036 loss only if certified local openings cover rent and bills.
feel: **Uneasy later**, secure in the next few years.
S4.quote: A timetable is useful only if a real boat and crew turn up.
fieldNote: He keeps **retirement timing** tied to verified numbers and actual work.
The **strong cushion** supports near-term security without assuming future deck shifts, retirement income or children’s wages.

steps.text: Keep maintaining ferry-ticket code while developer role pays
Save 240 monthly while both wages hold and request written retirement-income estimate
Enrol in available shore-safety course only if fee at most 160 and ten-month reserve intact
Seek certified paid local shore vacancies if displaced after 2036 and wages cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my ticketing wage could end before a qualified paid local shore opening appears. Written notice and a real bill-covering ferry vacancy would help us use savings deliberately.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I would buy a boat if software work ended. I would not put rent savings into a vessel without a paying job.

headlineQuote: I would not put rent savings into a vessel without a paying job.
portrait: Colin is a **58-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, higher pay and twelve months saved.
He and Bea **rent** while their grown children live separately.
He **uses AI daily** but checks tickets against the real passenger manifest.
He bounds **shore-safety training** with a fee cap and reserve before seeking certified paid work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his developer wage before a qualified shore vacancy appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and a real paid local ferry opening covering bills would help.
